newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures climbed for the third successive session as demand from investors moving money from the United States to Europe and domestic investors flush with liquidity overshadowed concerns about the state of French and German public finances, analysts said.
Traders said flow arguments probably accounted for much of the price movements as there was little news to justify the declines in yields seen in core European bond markets this week.
Some analysts said concerns about the French public deficit and the German political situation would probably resurface in the coming weeks when the buying pressure abated.
The September bond future climbed as high as 129.24, up 0.38, early in the session before trading in a fairly narrow range for the rest of the day and settling at 129.24.
Traders said the initial move higher on Wednesday looked overdone but the increase in Bund prices was pulling the French market higher and sparking short covering and triggering stops on the way up.
Technically the bulls' near-term target remained last week's high of 129.52 while solid support was seen at 128.82/84 an obstacle the contract hurdled in Tuesday's rally.

A trader at a U.S. house in Paris said one explanation for the outperformance of France and other European bonds was that investors were reversing trades in which they sold Europe for the United States to book profits before the end of June.
Analysts said optimism about a broad EMU start could justify the recent outperformance of Italian bonds but there was little reason why core European yields should be falling as well.

Stuart Thomson at Credit Agricole Indosuez said given the EMU uncertainties "you should get greater volatility and a steepening of yield curves in Europe, some convergernce with Germany but some convergence the other way as well".

Philippe Brossard, head of research a ABN Amro Finance, said if a report in today's Le Monde that the French 1997 deficit was heading for 3.6 percent of gross domestic product were true it could cause serious problems with Germany.

He said there also appeared to be a political problem brewing in Germany, with members of the ruling coalition pledging fierce resistance to any attempts to soften the three percent deficit criterion.
"I don't think it will be long before the political debate about Europe comes back," said Iain Lindsay, bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais.
Traders said the impression domestic investors were being forced to put excess cash to work in the bond market was also helping to support French bond prices.

They said many investors appeared to have put off buying bonds when a snap election was called in April and waited for yields to climb, but with levels of cash rising steadily they have had to buy bonds even though the market seems expensive.
"In France there's plenty of cash that needs to be invested. They've been waiting for a long time and most (investors) have limits on how much (cash) they can hold," Brossard said.
"There's certainly good demand kicking around when you prise it open," said a trader at a French bank.
PIBOR was supported for the second day running by non-resident buying and looked set to trade within a range of 96.55 and 96.63 in the short term, one trader said.
The French franc was stable at 3.3740 per mark compared with 3.3746 late on Tuesday.
